questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman presented with 2 days of bloody diarrhea. She worked as a school teacher and had led a school trip to a farm 4 days before her symptoms began. She had a history of mild asthma and used occasional salbutamol inhalers as needed. She had no known allergies. She had not received any recent steroids or antibiotics. On admission she was dehydrated. Her temperature was 36.8°C, and she was diffusely tender on abdominal examination. She had a seizure shortly after admission and developed some motor weakness. Investigations: Creatinine clearance 42 mL/min Peripheral white cell count 14.0 ×109/L Hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL Platelet count 90,000/μL CT scan abdomen findings consistent with pseudomembranous colitis Supportive management with IV fluids was commenced
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?
questions.explanation: Send stool for enteric pathogens (culture/NAAT) This patient has enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC, also called Shiga toxin-producing E. coli or STEC) causing bloody diarrhea following contact with a petting farm. This has caused hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) with renal failure, thrombocytopenia, and microangiopathic anemia. HUS can occur in 6%–9% of EHEC infections, and this patient also has neurologic symptoms. EHEC is also a rare cause of pseudomembranous colitis when culture-negative for Clostridioides difficile. Antibiotic treatment is contraindicated pending stool culture results and may make symptoms worse. Hence supportive treatment is advised. There are also likely to be other patients on the excursion who may be affected, and this should be further investigated as part of a possible outbreak.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q15

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presented with 3 days of diarrhea and severe abdominal pain. She was living in Texas but had traveled to Mexico to visit family 2 weeks prior to presentation. The patient reported drinking raw milk routinely and had a 3-year-old daughter in daycare. Investigations: Multiplex gastrointestinal panel PCR: positive for Shiga toxin 2
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Monitor for development of HUS Although E. coli O157 is the serotype most commonly associated with HUS, any serotype can cause HUS. There is no reason to rule out O157 since the patient should be monitored for HUS regardless of serotype. The presence of Shiga toxin 1 or Shiga toxin 2 is indicative of Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC), not Shigella. If Shigella was present, it would have been detected as Shigella. A Shigella-specific target is part of all currently available GI panels. Antimicrobial treatment of STEC has historically been associated with worse outcomes. There are some newer data that refute this dogma, but the standard practice is still to avoid antimicrobials for STEC.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q1

questions.model_answer:
a) Enterohemorrhagic E. coli O157:H7 is ingested (cattle are the major reservoir; undercooked beef, raw milk, contaminated produce or water). It is non-invasive and attaches to colonic epithelium by injecting its own translocated intimin receptor (Tir) into the host membrane, triggering assembly of actin pedestals (attaching-and-effacing lesion). It then elaborates Shiga-like toxin (Stx1 or Stx2), with Stx2 far more associated with HUS; toxin absorbed from the gut damages microvascular endothelium producing hemorrhagic colitis and HUS. H7 flagellin additionally activates proinflammatory signalling in colonic epithelial cells.
b) (1) Incubation 3-4 days after ingestion, with abdominal cramps and initially watery diarrhea that becomes grossly bloody. (2) Fever typically absent or minimal, unlike shigellosis or campylobacteriosis. (3) Sorbitol-negative colonies on sorbitol-MacConkey medium with O and H serotyping, and/or Shiga toxin detected in stool; HUS with thrombocytopenia may appear 2-4 days after diarrhea onset.
c) (1) Age extremes - children younger than 5 years and older adults. (2) Infection with a Stx2-producing strain rather than Stx1 alone. (3) Antibiotic exposure during the acute illness.
d) Antibiotics to which EHEC is susceptible (ampicillin, tetracycline, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, quinolones) induce the lysogenic phage carrying the toxin gene, increasing phage-mediated Shiga toxin production and release from injured organisms in the gut, so more toxin is available for absorption.
questions.beyond_mandell: Beyond the chapter's stated risk factors: cohort/clinical data also cite antimotility agent use and initial WBC >13 x10^9/L as HUS predictors.
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort gives an incubation of 1-10 days; Mandell states 3-4 days after ingestion.

cohort_answer.text: Pathogenesis: Shiga toxin production; STEC with Shiga toxin 2 and variants more virulent than Shiga toxin 1 alone. Clinical/lab features: incubation 1-10 days; initially nonbloody diarrhea becomes bloody 1-3 days after onset, often without persistent fever, usually abdo pain, typically resolves in 7 days; often elevated leuks and thrombocytosis. HUS risk factors: age (elderly >75 and younger than 10, also cited <5yrs/>65yrs), immunosuppression, use of antimotility agents in last 2 weeks, initial WBC >13, antibiotic use (highest if within first 3 days of illness). Antibiotics and HUS: in vitro, antibiotics cause E. coli to release Shiga toxin from injured bacteria in the intestine, making toxin more available for absorption

questions.model_answer:
a) Patient: (1) Place symptomatic residents on contact precautions in a private room with a dedicated commode/toilet, and cohort cases; (2) actively case-find with stool cultures/Shiga toxin testing on all residents with diarrhea and exclude symptomatic residents from group dining and communal activities. Staff: (1) Enforce hand hygiene with soap and water and gown/glove use for all care of symptomatic residents, with education and audit; (2) exclude symptomatic staff, especially food handlers, from work until asymptomatic and cleared. Environmental: enhanced cleaning and disinfection of high-touch surfaces, commodes and washrooms, plus review of food handling and the kitchen/water supply as the point source.
b) A propagated (person-to-person) epidemic curve - successive peaks roughly one incubation period apart with progressively larger case counts, rather than the single sharp peak of a point-source outbreak.
c) The interval between the peaks of successive case waves estimates the incubation period; for E. coli O157:H7 this is about 3 to 4 days.
questions.beyond_mandell: IPC specifics (contact precautions, cohorting, food-handler exclusion) follow PHAC/CDC long-term care enteric outbreak guidance; Mandell supports only hand hygiene, food handling, clean water and isolation of infected individuals.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Contact precautions with single-room placement or cohorting of symptomatic residents and a dedicated toilet/commode. (2) Active case finding with stool testing of all residents with diarrhea, and exclusion of symptomatic residents from communal dining and group activities.
b) (1) Hand hygiene with soap and water plus gown and gloves for all contact with symptomatic residents, reinforced by education and audits; dedicated staff cohorting to cases. (2) Exclusion of symptomatic staff, particularly food handlers, from work until asymptomatic and cleared.
c) Enhanced cleaning and disinfection of high-touch surfaces, washrooms and commodes, with review of food preparation and water supply.
d) Propagated (person-to-person) curve: successive waves of cases about one incubation period apart. Host factor: elderly, functionally dependent, often incontinent residents in close communal contact, allowing ongoing fecal-oral transmission. Pathogen factor: a very low infectious dose with prolonged fecal shedding, so secondary person-to-person spread occurs readily. Incubation period estimated from the interval between successive peaks, about 3 to 4 days.
questions.beyond_mandell: IPC bundle and low-infectious-dose/secondary-spread points rest on PHAC/CDC enteric outbreak guidance in long-term care; Mandell covers hand hygiene, food handling, clean water and isolation only.

questions.model_answer:
a) Resident: (1) Place symptomatic residents on contact precautions in a single room with dedicated toileting/commode until asymptomatic (and stool-negative if required). (2) Reinforce resident hand hygiene with soap and water before meals and after toileting, and restrict symptomatic residents from group activities and dining. Staff: (1) Exclude symptomatic staff from work until 48 hours after resolution of symptoms (food handlers per public health, often until stool-negative). (2) Enforce hand hygiene with soap and water plus gown and gloves for all care of symptomatic residents, with audit and education. Site: Close the unit to new admissions and transfers, halt the implicated food/water source, and perform enhanced environmental cleaning of washrooms and high-touch surfaces with a chlorine-based disinfectant.
b) A point-source (common-source, single-exposure) outbreak — a single sharp peak with a rise and fall spanning about one incubation period.
c) The incubation period is read from the interval between the point of exposure and the peak (and the range from the first to the last case), which for Escherichia coli O157:H7 is about 3-4 days, range 1-10 days.
d) Pathogen: production of Shiga toxin (Stx1/Stx2) by an enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli with the LEE/intimin attaching-and-effacing apparatus, together with a very low infectious dose (<100 organisms) permitting person-to-person spread. Host: a susceptible host — very young, elderly or immunocompromised, with reduced gastric acid barrier and no pre-existing immunity — who ingests the organism; presence of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) receptors on renal endothelium underlies progression to hemolytic uremic syndrome.

questions.model_answer:
a) Residents: (1) Place symptomatic residents on contact precautions in a single room with dedicated toileting/commode, and cohort cases if single rooms are unavailable. (2) Restrict movement — cancel group dining and group activities, restrict transfers and new admissions to the affected unit, and supervise resident hand hygiene before meals and after toileting.
Staff: (1) Cohort staff to affected versus unaffected residents, with hand hygiene using soap and water and gowns/gloves for all contact; (2) exclude symptomatic staff from work until asymptomatic (and screen/culture them), with education and no food handling while ill.
Environment: enhanced cleaning and disinfection of high-touch surfaces, bathrooms and commodes with an appropriate disinfectant at increased frequency, and review food handling/water source with removal of any implicated food.
b) (1) Confirm the outbreak exists and verify the diagnosis (compare with baseline; confirm isolates, consider molecular typing). (2) Establish a case definition and find cases systematically (line list by person, place, time; draw the epidemic curve). (3) Generate and test hypotheses about the source and mode of transmission (cohort or case-control study, environmental/food sampling). (4) Implement control measures and communicate/report findings to public health, then monitor for further cases and declare the outbreak over.
c) Host factor: susceptible elderly residents with immunosenescence, incontinence and dependence on staff for personal care, permitting ongoing person-to-person transmission (a propagated outbreak with successive generations of cases). Pathogen factor: a very low infectious dose with an incubation period of about 3-4 days, so cases cluster one incubation period apart — the q4d peaks correspond to successive generations of transmission rather than a point source.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Shiga toxin (Stx1/Stx2) release, whose A subunit depurinates 28S rRNA and halts host protein synthesis; (2) toxin binding to globotriaosylceramide on endothelial cells with intoxication and increased procoagulant expression; (3) microvascular thrombosis, causing mechanical RBC destruction, platelet consumption, and renal injury. b) (1) microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes; (2) thrombocytopenia; (3) acute renal failure. c) (1) young/pediatric age; (2) elderly age; (3) antimotility and antibiotic exposure. d) Antibiotic-induced cellular stress (e.g., fluoroquinolones, trimethoprim) induces high-level Shiga toxin production and lyses STEC, releasing more toxin; clinical data across multiple antibiotic classes link treatment to higher HUS risk.
questions.beyond_mandell: The cohort's 'high WBC at presentation' as a risk factor is not stated in this chapter (a recognized clinical predictor from the wider HUS literature).

cohort_answer.text:
E coli releases shiga toxin into bloodstream; Toxins causes endothelial damage especially in renal cells; Endothelial damage causes pro-coagulant and inflammatory cascade; Platelet form microthrombus at sites of damage thus blocking vessels; RBCs are destroyed when they flow through areas with mircothrombus, leading to haemolytic anaemia, schistocytes and renal damage
Thrombocytopenia; Elevated urea; Haemolytic anaemia; Bloody diarrhea
Age <5yo; Receiving abx; High WBC at presentation

questions.model_answer: EHEC produces Shiga toxin (Stx1/Stx2), whose pentameric B subunit binds globotriaosylceramide on host cells; after endocytosis the A subunit depurinates 28S rRNA, halting protein synthesis and triggering inflammation and apoptosis. Toxin binds leukocytes and disseminates in blood, intoxicating endothelial cells (notably renal), increasing procoagulant expression and provoking microvascular thrombosis. The resulting thrombotic microangiopathy causes mechanical hemolysis, platelet consumption/thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure.

cohort_answer.text: Shiga toxin released fro bacteria, damages endothelial cells that activates inflam/procoagulant factors/plt consumption. Also damages rbcs and tubular cells

questions.model_answer:
a) EHEC produces Shiga toxin (Stx1/Stx2). The pentameric B subunit binds globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) on endothelial cells, which are highly concentrated in the renal glomerulus; after endocytosis the A subunit depurinates 28S rRNA, halting host protein synthesis and injuring endothelium. This triggers inflammation/apoptosis, procoagulant expression, and platelet-fibrin microthrombi (thrombotic microangiopathy) producing the triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure.
b) (1) Extremes of age, especially children <5 years (and the elderly). (2) Antibiotic therapy (cellular stress, e.g. from fluoroquinolones/TMP, induces high Shiga-toxin levels). (3) Use of antimotility agents.
c) (1) Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes on peripheral smear. (2) Thrombocytopenia. (3) Acute kidney injury (rising creatinine/azotemia).

cohort_answer.text:
EHEC produces STX1 or STX2 toxins which bind GB3 receptors in endothelial cells, highly concentrated in renal tissue. These recruit leukocytes, can prompt apoptosis, elicit formation of microthrombi and impaired fibrinolysis; may also have secondary activation of complement
Antibiotic use (specifically fluoroquinolones) - due to increased release/production of toxin during diarrheal phase; High leukocyte count >13; <5 years old; Female; Vomiting; fever
